A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HOI benchmarking work, and their text, figures, tables and appendices are readable. The retained 1,274-image main benchmark and experiments can be matched despite extensive reorganization and the interchange of Settings 1 and 3.

before.justification: v2 reports original VLM and HOI-model evaluations, detector-assisted experiments and supervised fine-tuning results in Tables 2–4 and 6–7.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds cross-dataset experiments, ablations, annotation audits and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: The reported negative-screening rule changes: v2 Section 2.2 describes Qwen refinement with GPT-4o cross-checking rejected candidates; v3 Section 3.1 requires both models to judge a candidate incorrect before retaining it. The overall multiple-answer formulation and manual-refinement pipeline remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds V-COCO-based multi-person evaluation with 647 questions and SWiG-HOI-based human–human evaluation with 1,852 questions. It also adds explicit target human–object-pair tasks, whereas v2's localized evaluations target only the person. These substantially broaden evaluated populations and task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct to retained comparisons and evaluates ADA-CM and CMMP with ground-truth boxes in Setting 2, previously restricted to VLMs. The V-COCO-trained fine-tuning comparator disappears from the main-benchmark comparison but remains in the full-test comparison in Table 24.

E3.justification: New protocols include detecting or providing both human and object boxes, evaluating 9,546 full-test questions, varying Top-K and confidence thresholds, and excluding Qwen screening on a 12% subset. The reported Qwen2/2.5 resizing multiple also changes from 28 to 14. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun; swapping Settings 1 and 3 alone is renumbering.

E4.justification: v3 adds screening-agreement and circular-bias checks, option-position analysis, prediction-selection sensitivity, annotation audits, comparative failure taxonomies, cross-dataset robustness and full-test difficulty comparisons. These investigate substantially more questions than v2's detector and fine-tuning analyses. The earlier 68-class temporal-ambiguity inventory and V-COCO-trained head-bias panel are omitted.

E5.justification: Unlike v2's point estimates, v3 Table 7 reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 1,000 question-level resamples for four methods and two metrics in Setting 1. Appendix A.3 also newly reports inter-annotator agreement. These are limited additions to statistical reporting, without evidence of increased model-run counts.

E6.justification: Extensive new results accompany revisions to retained entries. Detection Macro-F1 changes from 57.25 to 50.71 for Qwen2.5-VL-32B and from 50.98 to 38.04 for InternVL3-38B, while their other columns remain unchanged (v2 Table 4; v3 Table 1). Fine-tuning scores and the main benchmark's multi-person percentage also change, the latter from 38.9% to 31.2%. These are reported revisions, not established performance losses.

T1.justification: The four metric definitions remain mathematically equivalent, moving from v2 Section 2.3 to v3 Appendix C. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs that are substantively revised.

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds large VLMs surpassing specialized methods on most metrics and claims to resolve annotation limitations. v3 qualifies performance as competitive or sometimes superior and describes mitigating annotation problems. Its central findings now emphasize complementary strengths, including HOI-model advantages in multi-action recognition and person attribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly limits MCQA to a diagnostic benchmark rather than a replacement for open-set generation. It adds explanations involving global attention, spatial topology, training-data scale and model capacity, while acknowledging unresolved causal contributions. New interpretations address domain shifts, concurrent-action omissions and predictions involving the wrong object.

D1.justification: v3 adds a repository link, screening prompt templates, four-annotator majority-vote procedures, LoRA target layers, five training epochs and batch size 32. It also documents object-pair prompts and licensing/access instructions for the additional datasets. These substantially improve disclosure; the newly specified fine-tuning details do not themselves establish a changed training method.

R1.justification: The cited literature expands substantially to additional HOI methods, fine-grained VLM recognition, hallucination, scaling, instruction tuning and downstream applications. Appendix A.2 newly distinguishes the benchmark from DAM and COCONut-PanCap and positions MCQA relative to open-set evaluation. This exceeds bibliographic updating or relocation of related work.

P1.justification: The title introduces CrossHOI-Bench, and the abstract, introduction and conclusions are substantially rewritten. Related work moves before benchmark construction, Settings 1 and 3 exchange numbers, and metric definitions and fine-tuning discussion move into reorganized appendices. These are extensive narrative and structural changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned with a multiple-choice illustration, and new construction diagrams, distribution plots, comparison charts and diagnostic tables substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing displays are also revised or relocated, including removal of the V-COCO panel from the fine-tuning figure.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's limited benchmark validation through screening and selection controls, annotation-agreement reporting, confidence intervals, object-pair evaluation and cross-dataset tests. Added implementation details and explicit MCQA limitations make the work more reproducible and its conclusions better qualified. Reporting defects remain, including stale setting references and inconsistent HOLa Macro-F1 values between Tables 1 and 7, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.
